title: Polymarket Halted International Trading After Hackers Drained Accounts
summary:
Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.
Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but the company said it will refund impacted traders.
The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company’s newer platform for people within the United States.
This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes.
In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.

title: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
summary:
Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.
Microsoft (MSFT) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet (GOOGL, GOOG) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short.
That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.
OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier.
Meta (META) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale.

title: Binance hacked for record $6.3 billion, withdrawals suspended after "complex attack"
summary:
Customer withdrawals have been temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses.
Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours.

Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X.

summary:

title: Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
summary:
It’s the first laptop, and only the second product overall, to support Apple CMF 2026 color modes.
The specification that’s been the standard for years is CIE 1931 (CIE stands for Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage, or International Commission on Illumination).
CIE 1931 doesn’t properly handle that and was created based on only 17 test subjects.
Apple CMF 2026 addresses that, so that displays look the same regardless of the technology they use.
Color science and display technologies have come a long way since 1931, when the CIE 1931 color space was established.

title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
summary:
With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models.
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token.
Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.

title: Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is $60 off just in time for sweater weather
summary:

Right now, Google’s fourth-gen Nest Learning Thermostat is on sale in all three colors for $219.99 ($60 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and The Home Depot, matching its best price of the year and just $10 shy of its all-time low.
Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is its most capable to date, and comes with new features designed to lower energy consumption without sacrificing comfort.
It can also suggest schedule changes to save energy and automatically adjusts the temperature when you’re away.
The Nest Learning Thermostat also improves on its predecessor with a beautifully designed adaptive display that shows your temperature settings, the weather, and the time from across the room.

title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
summary:
“A lot of people want local inference.
And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment.
And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

title: Battery Prototype Uses Superextensive Quantum Effects To Charge Faster
summary:
Although the term ‘quantum battery’ is a bit of a vague term, the cell that [Kieran Hymas] et al.
demonstrate in a recent paper does seem to suggest that it uses quantum effects to charge faster than would otherwise be possible, with this rate increasing faster than its volume, meaning at a superextensive rate.
The general idea behind a quantum battery is that these somehow use a quantum effect to store and release energy faster than would be possible using classical physics.
First proposed in 2013, the initial Dicke model saw its theoretical quantum advantage shot down by 2020, leading to the search for alternative models.
Effectively scaling up the cell would thus scale up the charge- and discharge rate faster than in a conventional chemical cell.
